passage:
Monday: Sachin and Farida took a one-page plan for the Saturday farewell party to their class teacher: 3 to 6 pm in the school hall. The teacher asked about supervision, the end time and travel home, and said the principal must approve too.

Wednesday: The principal signed. Farida wrote the parents' note with the time, the place, the end time of six, and a request to say who would collect each child. Sachin gathered the signed slips: twenty-eight of thirty-two.

Saturday: Two teachers sat at the back of the hall. At six, Farida read out the pick-up list at the gate, and each child left with someone on it. There was music and cake, and nothing else. Sachin was tired but pleased.

qa.q: How many signed slips did Sachin collect?
qa.a: Sachin collected twenty-eight of thirty-two signed slips.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel at the end of the party?
qa.a: Sachin felt tired but pleased, since the party ran safely to the agreed time.

qa.q: What could the organisers do about the four missing slips, and why?
qa.a: They could follow up with those four families before Saturday, because a child without a signed slip and a pick-up person should not be at risk.

qa.q: How might a parent see the pick-up request in the note?
qa.a: A parent likely feels reassured, since the note gives the end time, the place and a clear plan for getting the child home safely.

grounding: The organisers ask the teacher and parents for permission, agree an end time, keep the venue supervised, arrange safe travel home and avoid anything that could put guests at risk.

passage:
Sonali beta, you're asking me how to plan your class picnic? Then listen to your Bhupen mama's story first.

When I was seventeen in Guwahati, a few of us wanted a riverside Bihu party for our class. My first idea was: go at night, tell nobody, bring a big speaker. My friend's father heard and just asked, "And if someone slips into the river in the dark?" I had no answer.

So we did it properly. Our class teacher agreed and came along. Every parent signed a slip. We fixed the end at six, before dark. We picked the flat bank near the ghat where the boatmen could see us, kept everyone away from the deep side, and arranged two autos to drop the girls home in groups.

It felt less wild. But every single person got home safe.

qa.q: What time did the party have to end?
qa.a: They fixed the end at six, before dark.

qa.q: How did young Bhupen feel when asked what would happen if someone slipped into the river?
qa.a: He felt caught out and a little embarrassed, because he had no answer to such an obvious danger.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed the plan, and what would have happened without it?
qa.a: The friend's father's question about the dark river changed it; without it, the class might have gone at night with no adults and real risk.

qa.q: How might the parents who signed the slips have felt about the picnic?
qa.a: They likely felt reassured and able to say yes, because a teacher was present, there was a clear end time and the travel home was arranged.

grounding: An elder recalls organisers asking teacher and parents for permission, setting an end time, keeping the place supervised and arranging safe travel home.

passage:
The farewell party for Class 12 had one problem nobody had budgeted for: the only free venue, the school terrace, closed at dusk and had a low parapet.

Neelam, head of the organising group, sat with Usha in the empty classroom, the power cut making the fan still. They had three days and almost no money.

"We can't just sneak up there after dark," Neelam said, rubbing her eyes. Usha nodded and started a list by candlelight.

They asked the vice-principal, who agreed to a four-to-seven slot if two teachers stayed. They marked a chalk line two metres from the parapet and assigned volunteers to watch it. Parents got a message with the end time. For the few who lived far, Usha matched them with classmates' families driving the same way.

The party was shorter than people wanted. Nobody complained on the way home.

qa.q: What slot did the vice-principal agree to?
qa.a: The vice-principal agreed to a four-to-seven slot if two teachers stayed.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she said they couldn't sneak up after dark?
qa.a: Neelam seems uneasy about the risk and determined to do things properly despite the pressure of time and money.

qa.q: What else could the organisers do to make the terrace safer?
qa.a: They could ask for the terrace lights to be checked and keep a first-aid kit and a teacher's phone number handy, which adds protection at little cost.

qa.q: How might a student who lived far away see this plan?
qa.a: That student might feel relieved and cared for, because Usha matched them with a family driving the same way instead of leaving them to find a lift alone.

grounding: Shows organisers, under time and money pressure, getting permission, setting an end time, keeping supervision, avoiding a risky edge and arranging safe travel home.
